content:
Special Master Jose Linares rejected the Department of Justice's motion for reconsideration of his decision allowing Apple to seek documents from 14 government agencies. Here are the details.

A bit of background

In the DOJ's antitrust lawsuit against Apple, one of Apple's defense strategies involves the U.S. government's own use of its products.

Apple's basic argument is that some of the practices the DOJ is challenging are actually reasonable security and privacy safeguards. To support this defense, Apple wants to know how federal agencies evaluate security and privacy when forming smartphone policies and making procurement decisions.

To that end, Apple has been trying to obtain documents from the following 14 agencies:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

After Apple initially moved to compel the agencies to produce documents, the DOJ objected. The dispute was then referred to Special Master Jose Linares for a ruling.

Last month, Linares granted Apple's request, prompting the DOJ to file a motion for reconsideration. The DOJ argued that he applied the wrong legal standard, that Apple's requests were overly burdensome and disproportionate, and that the documents sought had only limited relevance to the case.

Apple then filed an opposition, arguing that the DOJ's motion was "without merit in any respect" and rebutting the DOJ's arguments point by point.

Linares has now issued a new decision, ruling that "none of the arguments the DOJ has raised in support of its motion for reconsideration is persuasive," and he upheld the original ruling.

Apple is allowed to seek documents

The new decision states:

The decision adds that Linares believed that "in any event, there is no persuasive reason at this stage to change course," and that "in this case, the federal agencies are part of the United States for purposes of party discovery."

Excerpts from the decision:

Plaintiff attempts to split hairs by asserting, under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 45, that "non-parties to a lawsuit enjoy greater protection from discovery than parties." [...] Plaintiff therefore concludes that the Special Master's order and opinion rely on faulty reasoning because they do not cite or incorporate Rule 45 into the analysis. The Special Master is intimately familiar with Rule 45 and the different standards applicable to third-party discovery. A cursory review of the Special Master's opinion and order reveals that plaintiff is wholly incorrect. In fact, the Special Master already explained at length how this dispute arose. [...]. A review of that portion of the opinion and order shows that plaintiff itself is the reason why defendant was required to issue subpoenas.

The document further explains that Linares found the 14 federal agencies to be part of the United States, rather than third parties that would normally enjoy additional protections under Rule 45:

The document also said the DOJ "misunderstands the legal framework applicable to this dispute," while criticizing its claim that the relevance of the requested information is "slight" as made "without citing any basis."

As a result, Apple is once again allowed to seek documents from the 14 federal agencies.
